overview: The Palas built a major kingdom in Bengal and Bihar from the mid-eighth century, linking royal power with Buddhist monasteries and international learning. This map starts in 700, before their rise, and runs to 1200, beyond their main imperial power. Its broad repeated outlines cannot show every conquest, rebellion or rival.

periods.title: Before the dynasty
periods.summary: The imported map begins before Gopala founded Pala rule.

periods.title: Rise and expansion
periods.summary: Gopala, Dharmapala and Devapala established a major eastern Indian power.

periods.title: Changing fortunes
periods.summary: Succession disputes and rivals weakened the kingdom before Mahipala I renewed its strength.

periods.title: Restoration and rebellion
periods.summary: Mahipala I and later Ramapala restored territories, with rebellions between their reigns.

periods.title: Successor kingdoms
periods.summary: Sena expansion displaced Pala authority in Bengal; later Bihar namesakes have uncertain dynastic connections.

items.text: Dharmapala’s Khalimpur charter celebrates his installation of a king at Kannauj. It presents other rulers as respectfully accepting his choice. That is the court’s triumphant account of an ambitious intervention, useful evidence for how the dynasty advertised power across northern India.

Another verse imagines the king’s praises sung by cattle keepers, forest dwellers, villagers, playing children and market officials watching the weights. Even caged parrots join in! This is royal publicity, but the poet’s imagined audience brings courtyards, markets and ordinary work into an inscription about a king.

A ninth-century copperplate records an international request: Balaputradeva, ruler of Suvarnadvipa, had established a monastery at Nalanda and sought support from Devapala. Five villages were assigned to its upkeep. Religious learning could connect a local farming community to a patron from far away.

Those villages included pasture, watering places, mango and mahua trees, and rights to revenues. Residents were still instructed to deliver their dues. A grand donation therefore changed who received agricultural resources; the monastery’s books and meals depended on people continuing to farm.

The same Nalanda grant provided for food, robes, bedding, copying religious works and building repairs. It even specified cloth held as a fund for medicine for sick residents. Learning required practical support: someone had to feed the scholars, maintain the roof and care for illness.

At Somapura Mahavihara, now Paharpur in Bangladesh, a vast quadrangle surrounded the central shrine. Its last building phase had 177 cells. These rooms show the scale of monastic residence, although counting rooms does not tell us exactly how many people lived or studied there.

The central shrine rose in a cross-shaped plan, with a route for walking around it. Bands of terracotta reliefs decorated its walls. Dharmapala’s name appears on a clay seal from the site, tying this enormous brick complex to the dynasty’s early patronage.

Excavators identified a likely cooking establishment west of the monastery’s dining area. A large hall had a narrow surrounding corridor; ashes and charcoal were concentrated toward its western end. Archaeology can sometimes find the kitchen long after the last meal has disappeared.

Three large wells stood in a row near the kitchen and dining area, probably supplying their water. A masonry drain nearby was traced for more than 150 feet. Feeding a large monastic community meant organizing water and waste as well as religious lessons.

The main temple had drainage channels beneath its passageways and terrace. One outlet emptied through the mouth of a stone gargoyle before another drain carried the water away. The carved creature had a practical job: spectacular architecture still needed somewhere for water to go.

Making a palm-leaf book was skilled work. The leaves were soaked, dried, polished with a conch shell and trimmed; holes allowed a binding cord to pass through. A scribe left spaces for paintings among the long lines of writing. The page had to be prepared before the first letter.

Painters worked with colors including indigo blue, cinnabar red, chalk white and black from lamp soot. They added shading and fine outlines to tiny figures. Copying and decorating a manuscript could also honor parents and teachers: donors sought religious merit for loved ones as well as themselves.

A surviving twelfth-century palm-leaf page depicts Green Tara seated on a cushion, one hand offering protection. The entire leaf is only about five centimeters tall but more than fifty-five centimeters long. Think of fitting a carefully painted sacred scene onto a very narrow strip of a school desk.

Another painted page, dated about 1090, shows the Buddha protecting mariners. Religious art gave visual form to hopes for safety on dangerous journeys. Below, a bodhisattva in a cave plays a vina, a stringed instrument: even a small manuscript page could hold a sea voyage and music.

Atisha, an abbot of Vikramashila, traveled to Tibet in 1042 to teach. A later Tibetan portrait shows him holding a bound palm-leaf manuscript, with a yellow hat marking scholarly achievement. Made in the twelfth century, that image records his lasting authority across the mountains.

sections.title: A small piece of their writing

items.text: Devapala’s ninth-century Nalanda seal reads “śrī-devapāla-devasya”: “Of illustrious Devapāladeva.” This is the scholarly Roman transliteration of Sanskrit originally written in Siddhamatrika script. The associated charter dates itself to his thirty-fifth regnal year, giving the short ownership label a precise place within his reign.

ending.text: Sena rulers displaced Pala power in Bengal during the twelfth century, while remnants persisted in Bihar. The map’s 1200 endpoint is not a single empire-wide collapse. Monastic learning, artistic traditions and the region’s communities continued through changing rulers.
